references.text: Moses predicted that God would raise up a prophet whom the people should listen to. In [ref:5 Mos 18:15-19|Deuteronomy 18:15-19], the duty to heed God's word through Moses and the prophets is emphasized—precisely the point Abraham makes in the parable: they have Moses and the prophets, and that should be sufficient.

[ref:Jes 8:20|Isaiah 8:20] points to the testimony of the Law and the Prophets as the decisive test. If people do not hold to this word, it is "because there is no light in them"—a principle that reflects Abraham's answer that Moses and the prophets are sufficient.

Jesus says in [ref:Joh 5:45-47|John 5:45-47] that Moses wrote about him, and that whoever does not believe Moses' writings will not believe Jesus' words either. This is a direct parallel to Luke 16:31, where the point is that whoever does not listen to Moses and the prophets will not be convinced even by someone rising from the dead.

In [ref:Joh 12:10-11|John 12:10-11], the chief priests planned to kill Lazarus after he had been raised from the dead, instead of believing. This illustrates Jesus' point in the parable: even a resurrection from the dead does not convince those who refuse to listen to God's word.

The raising of Lazarus in [ref:Joh 11:43-48|John 11:43-48] is a striking example that someone actually did rise from the dead, yet the religious leaders were still not convinced—they instead planned to put Jesus to death. A literal fulfillment of the words in Luke 16:31.

In [ref:Apg 17:30-32|Acts 17:30-32], Paul preaches about the resurrection on the Areopagus, but many mocked and refused to believe. The message of one who rose from the dead did not convince those unwilling to listen—again confirming Abraham's words.

Paul testifies in [ref:Apg 26:22-23|Acts 26:22-23] that he says nothing other than what Moses and the Prophets said would happen: that the Messiah should suffer, rise from the dead, and proclaim light. Here the resurrection is directly linked to the testimony of Moses and the Prophets, exactly as Luke 16:31 does.

The risen Jesus rebukes the disciples in [ref:Luk 24:25-27|Luke 24:25-27] for being slow to believe all that the prophets had spoken, and he explains from Moses and all the Prophets what concerned him. The testimony of Scripture remains the foundation even after the resurrection.

[ref:Rom 10:16-17|Romans 10:16-17] states that not all obeyed the gospel, and that faith comes from hearing the message—namely Christ's word delivered through Scripture. Those who do not hear the Word will not be convinced by signs either.

In [ref:Luk 16:29-30|Luke 16:29-30], Abraham says that his brothers have Moses and the Prophets to listen to, but the rich man insists that someone rising from the dead would convince them. Verse 31 is the decisive answer to this dialogue.
